opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think my feelings about it have shifted a lot over the years. A lot of that early work, things like neural module networks, was built on the bet that you could take the compositional structure that's visible in language and use it more or less directly to structure the computation a model does. If a question asks "what color is the thing to the left of the cylinder," you parse that, and the parse tells you which little modules to assemble: find the cylinder, shift attention left, describe the color. The world, in some sense, was assumed to factor the same way the sentence did.

Looking back, I'd say some of those assumptions held up and some really didn't. The part that didn't was the idea that we as designers needed to hard-code that structure, that you had to hand the model a parser and a fixed inventory of module types and say, here's how reasoning decomposes. What we've learned since then, very forcefully, is that big models trained on enough data discover a lot of that structure on their own, and often a more flexible version of it than what we would have written down. So the specific architectural commitments look, in hindsight, somewhat over-engineered.

But I don't think the underlying intuition was wrong. The thing I still believe is that compositionality is a real property of both language and the world, and that models generalize well to the extent that they capture it somehow. The question has really moved from "how do we build structure in" to "how do we find out whether the structure is there, and what do we do when it isn't." A lot of my more recent work on interpretability and on what models know about the world is really a continuation of that same question, just approached from the other side. Instead of imposing the decomposition, we look inside and ask whether the model has built something like it.

And I'd say there's a humility lesson in there too. In grounding work especially, there was a tendency to assume we knew what the right representation of the environment was, objects, relations, actions, and to evaluate everything in those terms. Sometimes the world as the data presents it is messier than that, and the most interesting failures were exactly the cases where our assumed structure didn't match what the task needed. So I see the early work less as a set of answers and more as a set of hypotheses that turned out to be useful scaffolding, even if we've since taken a lot of the scaffolding down.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the structural assumptions were doing most of the work, and that's both the thing I'd defend about that era and the thing I'd criticize about it.

If you go back to the semantic parsing and instruction-following work I was doing early on, the setup was almost always something like: there's a world, the world has a fixed set of objects and relations, there's a fixed logical form or a fixed planning language, and the job of the model is to map a sentence onto something in that space. The structure of the environment was handed to the model by me, by the person building the benchmark. And once you've done that, a lot of the hard questions about what grounding even means have already been answered. You've decided what counts as an object, what counts as an action, what the primitive predicates are. The model is doing composition over things that were already carved up for it.

The thing that was good about that is that it made certain phenomena very legible. You could actually ask, does this model generalize compositionally? Does it handle a verb it saw once in a new argument structure? Those questions are hard to even pose if you don't have some latent structure to point at. And I still think a lot of the intuitions from that work turned out to be right in spirit, that language is a fairly sparse, fairly abstract signal and that a lot of the leverage comes from the fact that it decomposes.

What I got wrong, or at least what I was too confident about, was the idea that the structure had to be built in rather than discovered. The implicit bet was that you needed to give the model the ontology because it wasn't going to find it on its own from data. And then the last several years happened, and it turned out that if you have enough text and a reasonably general model, a lot of that structure shows up anyway, often in a form that's messier than what I would have written down but also more flexible and more faithful to how people actually use words. So in retrospect the assumptions were a crutch. They were a way of getting something to work when the models were weak, and I think I sometimes mistook them for claims about how language works.

The other thing I'd say is that the environments were small in a way that let us fool ourselves. In a block world or a navigation grid, the set of things you can possibly mean is tiny, so grounding looks like a lookup problem. In the actual world it's not. The hard part of grounding isn't attaching a word to a referent, it's figuring out which aspects of a situation are even relevant to the thing someone said, and the toy environments basically assumed that away.

So my current view is something like: those assumptions were the right scaffolding at the time, they let us ask sharp questions, but the interesting work now is in figuring out which pieces of structure you still want to impose, maybe for interpretability or for data efficiency, and which pieces you should just let the model find. I'm much more agnostic about that than I was ten years ago.

astra-6.text:
I think those assumptions were doing a lot of work. We often started with a world where we already knew what the objects were, what actions were available, and something about the structure of the task. Then we asked how language could connect to those things. That’s a useful way to isolate a question, but it also means you’ve supplied part of what you eventually want a learning system to discover.

The part I still find compelling is the idea that language has compositional structure, and that this structure can help organize perception and action. If I understand the pieces of an instruction, I should be able to put them together in a way that lets me do something new. But that doesn’t necessarily mean we should prescribe a particular inventory of symbols or a particular computational structure in advance.

So I’d distinguish the hypothesis from the machinery we used to explore it. The hypothesis is that structure matters for learning and generalization. The machinery often made quite strong assumptions about what that structure ought to be. Looking back, the interesting question is how much of it can be learned, and what kinds of supervision or interaction make that possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they were useful assumptions, but they also did a lot of the work. In those early settings, we often decided in advance what the relevant objects and actions were, or what kinds of compositional structure the model should use. Then the learning problem was to connect language to that structure.

That let us ask a fairly precise question: if you give a learner the right pieces, can it learn how language puts those pieces together? But success on that question doesn’t tell you how the learner discovers the pieces in the first place, or whether those are the right pieces for a less controlled environment.

So I’d view that work as studying one part of the problem under strong simplifying assumptions. I still think the compositionality questions are valuable. What I’d be more cautious about is treating the structure we supplied as something we’d explained, rather than something we’d assumed.
